introduction.text: The Basilica di Santa Pudenziana al Viminale is Rome’s oldest surviving Christian basilica, originally a 2nd‑century house that was converted into a church in the 4th century. Its early mosaics, Romanesque architecture, and association with early Christian figures make it a key monument of the Christian heritage of the city.

history.description: The original shrine building dates from the 2nd century, built as the house of the Roman senator Quintus Cornelius Pudens.
The basilica was erected during the reign of Pope Pius I, around 140–155.
The basilica served as the official residence of the Pope until 313 AD, when Emperor Constantine the Great offered the Lateran Palace as a church.
During the pontificate of Pope Siricius (384–399) the building was transformed into a Christian basilica.
In 499 the basilica was recognized by a synod and allowed to administer the Holy Sacraments.
Romanesque architecture and a belltower were added in the early 13th century.
A major restoration was carried out in 1388 by Francesco da Volterra.
Current renovations are underway and are scheduled to complete in 2027.

design.description: The basilica incorporates Roman thermae bath walls, especially on the right side, dating to the reign of Hadrian (117–138).
The nave columns are original from the early structure, and the 13th‑century Romanesque belltower was added by Francesco da Volterra.
The façade features a marble frieze from the 11th century, depicting Pastore, Pudentiana, Praxedes, and Pudens.

art.description: A late‑antique mosaic in the apse, dating to the end of the 4th century, shows Christ enthroned with apostles and symbolic evangelist figures.
Frescoes by Pomarancio and Pietro Gagliardi adorn the dome and façade, respectively.
The Chapel of Saint Peter contains a wooden relic of the altar table used by Saint Peter, and a bronze crucifix by Achille Tamburini.
